speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) goes some way, I think, to substantiate or support a ruling along the lines of that which I understand Your Honour has in mind. I think, however, there are one or two other observations which should be made. The citation which I think is applicable in this case is citation 182 of Beauchesne's third edition dealing with the question of anticipation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO PROMOTE AND ACCELERATE ACTIVITY
speechtext: Would the hon. member be good enough to repeat the number of the citation? I did not hear it.

subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE TO PROMOTE AND ACCELERATE ACTIVITY
speechtext:
It is citation No. 182 found at page 79 of Beauchesne's third edition which I think reproduces the paragraph from Campion which Your Honour has just referred us to.
As I said, I think there are a couple of points which should be decided before that citation is applied to its full extent. Obviously the rule against anticipation should not be invoked with respect to two motions which are different in substance, and I suggest to Your Honour that there are sufficient differences between these two motions to raise a doubt as to whether in fact the one anticipates the other. That is, the motion of the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) calls for the setting up of a committee to inquire into the field of research generally and it would also give that committee specific powers, the most important power being that of calling for witnesses and sending for documents and papers. That provision is conspicuously omitted from the motion standing in the name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). Furthermore, the motion of the minister is confined to the field of non-military research. I do not find any such restriction in the motion of the hon. member for Lambton West, so there are, I submit, very substantial and important differences between the two motions sufficient to raise a real question as to whether the one does anticipate the other.
The other point that I think it is important to have settled quite conclusively is this, Mr. Speaker. I am quite sure that you and all hon. members would agree with me when I say that the rule against anticipation was not intended to be used-and should not be so used-to give the government, whatever

government it might be, the opportunity to block discussion of a private member's motion which chronologically anticipated the government's notice of motion simply by placing on the order paper a motion in similar terms and then not proceeding with it. That is what happened last year.
I looked up the record, and I would refer Your Honour to page 1353 of Hansard of last year where the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) withdrew his motion on the basis of a previous assurance from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that the government intended to set up and proceed with a committee on research. The government did not proceed with its motion that year.
As I say, I think some regard must be had for the chronological order in which these motions appear on the order paper. Otherwise the broad application of the principle we are now discussing would enable the government effectively to block discussion by the simple device of placing a motion on the order paper and then not proceeding with it.
I recognize that to a considerable extent we have had an assurance from the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) today, but with all deference to yourself and to the right hon. gentleman I suggest that we should have the most absolute assurance that the government will in fact proceed at this session with the motion standing in the name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, not merely that it is the present intention of the government to do so. For my part I would hope that Your Honour would give effect to the first point I made, namely that these motions are different in substance and that therefore one does not anticipate the other. But should Your Honour disagree with me on that point I think it is proper to ask that Your Honour should obtain from the Prime Minister the most specific assurance on the other point, namely that the government will proceed with this other motion at this session before you apply the rule against anticipation.

subsubtopic: HARMLESS POISONOUS GASES EMITTED BY ENGINES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of taking

steps to further protect the health of the nation by requiring all trucks, tractors, buses, or any other diesel-powered vehicles, including engines on railway lines, and all stationary type of engines, be equipped with a device to render harmless, poisonous gases emitted from the exhaust of such vehicles or engines.
He said:	I move this resolution, Mr. Speaker, because I believe that diesel and gasoline fumes are a very definite menace to the health of the nation, and especially so in districts of concentrated population. I make no apology for bringing it to the attention of hon. members, even though I realize that control measures may more properly be a matter to come under provincial jurisdiction.
It is my sincere hope that through the discussion of this resolution we may bring about a general awareness of the dangers we encounter in the air we breathe.
Canadians have fought hard for the pure food laws that guarantee that our food is uncontaminated. We have organized and paid for expensive water systems that assure us of a plentiful supply for pure water. There have been many debates on the question of whether our drinking water should be fluori-nated to prevent tooth decay. But until quite recently practically nothing has been done about the air we breathe. The acute effects of unrestricted air pollution upon public health have been demonstrated unpleasantly but successfully in three air pollution disasters, namely, the Meuse valley in Belgium in 1930; Donora, Pennsylvania, in 1948; and Poza Rica, Mexico, in 1950.
The chronic effects of air pollution are not so clearly defined, but nevertheless the frequent occurrence of eye irritation during periods of smog in Los Angeles and statistics on the increase in the death rate from respiratory diseases during fogs in industrial communities in England represent evidence which cannot be ignored. Although this resolution deals specifically with diesel fumes I should like to discuss for a few minutes the possible effects of high concentrations of exhaust fumes from gasoline-burning engines.
In the case of Los Angeles, California, of which we have heard so much recently in the press, the smog condition is to a large degree caused by the exhaust fumes of motor vehicles. Dr. Haagen-Smit, a biochemist, in trying to solve the problem in Los Angeles proved that nitrogen dioxide, a product of all combustion, serves as a catalyst converting the atmospheric oxygen into its unstable form of ozone in the presence of sunshine, and proved further that smog was a result of the reaction of ozone with gasoline vapour. In the Los Angeles area there are some 2-3 million motor vehicles circulating
Health-Poisonous Gases almost daily. The quantity of unburned gasoline or gasoline vapour emitted from those vehicles is estimated to be 1,200 tons daily.
It is a well known fact that the mileage per gallon of gasoline decreases considerably in stop and go city traffic. At cruising speed about 250 parts per million of the total exhaust is unburned gasoline vapour. When a motor is idling it is two or three times that figure, but when you lift your foot off the accelerator and decelerate, the output is 5,000 parts per million. It is generally conceded that about 7 per cent of gasoline is unburned, and that figure could be increased to 8 or 9 per cent through evaporation from the carburetor or fuel tank.
This problem is one which we must face in the near future as the number of motor vehicles increases in Canada. Far more important is the fact that deadly gases are emitted with these exhaust fumes. One of these gases is known as carbon monoxide, with which the average motorist is only vaguely familiar. We may attribute this lack of familiarity to the fact that he can neither smell it, taste it, feel it nor hear it; yet in a very short space of time it can be the means of reducing the mental functions of a driver to the point where co-ordination of muscles and the ability to react properly in the operation of a vehicle to below even minimum requirements for safety.
A concentration of -02 to -03 per cent of carbon monoxide will cause a headache; a concentration of -04 to -07 per cent, unconsciousness; and a concentration of -08 to [DOT]10 per cent, death. Unlike some poisons it does not permit a human being to build up immunity over a period of time. Repeated exposures, particularly attacks of acute poisoning, result in a progressive increasing susceptibility to the gas and can cause acute cumulative tissue damage.
It might be well to pursue the theory that carbon monoxide is the cause of a great many accidents on our highways due to the inefficiency of drivers. At some time all of us have experienced a condition of sleepiness while driving our motor vehicles. We have also perceived odors from our own car and cars in front of us. We have experienced headaches, dizziness and sometimes car sickness. Whenever any of these occur while you are driving, consider carbon monoxide and bear in mind that death by carbon monoxide is not restricted to tightly-closed garages with the motor running and that a state of collapse has occurred when cars are parked with their motors running in some instances even while they are travelling along the highway. It is safe to assume that

Health-Poisonous Gases carbon monoxide has contributed a great deal to many accidents heretofore classed as unexplained.
To substantiate this the California highway patrol tested 1,007 automobiles on the open highway and found that 30 cars contained concentrations of this gas in excess of the maximum safe limit. The conclusion arrived at from the survey showed that 3 per cent of the cars tested were found to have concentrations of carbon monoxide in such quantity as would affect the driver with headache, sleepiness, weakness, impaired judgment, and decrease his driving ability for a period of several hours. Another conclusion was that no automobile, regardless of design, age or type, is free from the possibility of carbon monoxide entering the driver or passenger compartment. It behooves every motorist to have his car tested for complete exhaust system tightness and to observe the rules of safety at all time in order to rule out as much as possible the dangers of this lethal gas which is an inherent part of our present-day motor vehicle.
If this condition exists on the open highway, what is the situation in areas of highly concentrated traffic. Tests have been taken in these areas and on busy streets and concentrations of -09 per cent have been found during periods of high temperature and humidity. I have just indicated that a concentration of -09 per cent will cause death. Here we have concentrations of -09 per cent on busy streets during heavy traffic hours with high temperature and humidity.
Is it any wonder that the busy housewife often comes home from a shopping trip with a splitting headache? Then consider a busy street with high buildings on either side, with many of the offices equipped with air conditioners in their windows. These fumes rise and infiltrate into the offices and that is probably the reason why many secretaries have bottles of headache tablets on their desks.
Unlike the gasoline engine the diesel engine operates normally with excess air. The fuel is injected into the cylinder and is ignited by virtue of the pressure and temperature in the cylinder rather than by a spark. The fuel used is heavier than gasoline and has a higher boiling range. Because of the excess air used, very little of the fuel is normally exhausted unburned. Under certain conditions of operation, however, both smoke and aldehydes are evolved. The latter are quite noticeable when in high concentrations because of their pungent odour and eye-irritation characteristics.

summary of the reported variation in diesel exhaust gas composition.

The odour and irritating effects of the exhaust gas of diesel engines are caused mainly by aldehydes, which occur in varying amounts depending on several factors, such as the fuel, the air ratio at which the engine is operating, the design of the engine, engine temperature, and the condition of the fuel injection equipment or mechanism. If the exhaust gas contains a high concentration of aldehydes, it is definitely irritating to the eyes and nasal passages; in fact, the irritating effect may be more noticeable than the odour if one is exposed to a high concentration of the exhaust gas.
But the most dangerous gas in diesel fumes, both with regard to injury to health and amount produced, is oxides of nitrogen, which when inhaled form nitric and nitrous acids in the respiratory organs. Let us compare oxides of nitrogen with carbon monoxide, as far as toxicity is concerned. An atmosphere containing -5 to 10 per cent of carbon monoxide is likely to be fatal to human beings in less than 30 minutes of exposure, whereas as little as -07 per cent of oxides of nitrogen may cause fatalities in the same length of
[Mr. Charlton.)

time. This is an indication of the danger from the exhaust gas of diesel engines as compared with gasoline engines.
There is still another danger from these exhaust fumes which science is presently dealing with.
Dr. W. C. Hueper of the cancer control branch, national cancer institute of the United States public health service, addressed the first Canadian cancer conference which took place in June 1954, under the sponsorship of the National Cancer Institute of Canada. I quote from certain comments of his which I feel will be of interest to you:
Comments on respiratory aromatic hydrocarbons. At the present time, exposure to tar, pitch, asphalt, heavy fuel oils, lubricating and cutting oils, soot from domestic furnaces, incinerators, industrial power plants, oil refineries, steel plants, metal smelters, carbon black factories, oil dumps, and smudge pots, as well as to the effluents of diesel and gasoline engines represents the most widespread occupational environment contact with carcinogenic material.
Since our civilization and economical life has been built around the production and use of the basic carbonaceous substances and their derivatives, it does not seem feasible to attain complete protection against exposure to these carcinogenic chemicals with the preventive and prophylatic engineering and sanitary measures practical and economical at the present time.
There is, however, no doubt that a great deal remains to be done in this respect and that we are still rather far removed from having the maximal amount of possible reduction in exposure to the respiratory cancer producing hydrocarbons contained in the various carbonaceous substances mentioned.
I also have here an article entitled "Aromatic Hydrocarbons" which appeared in "Industrial Hygiene and Occupational Medicine", 11th volume, on pages 113 to 120, in February 1955. This article was written by Paul Kotin, M.D., Hans L. Falk, Ph.D., and Marilyn Thomas, B.A. I should like to deal with the comments and the summary and conclusions of this article. I might say that it is an article having to do with the testing of mice with aromatic hydrocarbon from diesel engine exhaust. It states:
Demonstration of carcinogenic hydrocarbons in the exhaust products of diesel engines and the successful production of skin tumours by the painting of diesel-engine exhaust extracts is selfexplanatory in so far as satisfying the criteria for proof of experimental carcinogenicity. The emission of carcinogenic hydrocarbons into the atmosphere from diesel engines is of particular interest from a preventive medicine and public health point of view. The as yet unaccomplished task of relating proved experimental carcinogenic hydrocarbons to human lung cancer in no way militates against regarding their atmospheric presence as anything but a potential hazard. While it is apparent that diesel engine exhaust does not differ markedly from gasoline engine exhaust and incinerator soots, its possible control presents a brighter picture. The present inability to eliminate cacinogenic hydrocarbon emissions into the atmosphere from the latter two sources is not duplicated

Efficient and innocuous operation of a diesel engine from an atmospheric pollution viewpoint is possible without costly engine redesign or the development of catalytic or combustion completing devices for inclusion in the exhaust systems, a situation not applicable to incinerator or gasoline engine pollution sources.
The qualitative presence of chrysene and Compound Y in the exhaust products of a diesel engine was unanticipated in view of their absence from gasoline engine exhausts. The knowledge that these two compounds can be emitted into the atmosphere incidental to rubber tire wear and tear precludes the conclusion that the diesel engine is alone responsible for their presence.
As noted in our previous publications, the qualitative studies reported herein are in the process of repetition by means of injection in contrast to painting techniques, with quantitation of both individual components of the exhaust samples and combinations of emitted hydrocarbons serving as the basis for the experiments.
Here are the summary and conclusions:
The particulate phase of diesel-engine exhaust products has been analysed. Carcinogenic hydrocarbons have been demonstrated as being present among these products. Their production under varying conditions of engine operation has been determined.
Extracts of the particulate phase of the exhaust products have been successfully used in painting experiments to produce skin papillomas in C57 black mice and cancers in A strain mice. The demonstration of carcinogenic hydrocarbons in a source of atmospheric pollution and their successful use for the production of skin tumors in mice require their careful assessment relative to a possible role in the observed increasing frequency of human lung cancer. Two observations are worthy of special comment: first, the high yield of aromatic polycyclic hydrocarbons, including benzpyrene from the exhaust of an inefficiently operating diesel engine; second, the increase in these emissions as the load and engine speed are increased. This is in marked contrast to a gasoline engine where load and speed increase reduce the amount of aromatic polycyclic hydrocarbons, emitted into the air.
I have here a statement made in London by Sir Clement Price Thomas, a distinguished British surgeon who took part in the lung operation performed on King George VI in 1951. The press release states that Sir Thomas declared that smoking does not cause cancer of the lung:
He said the fact that lung cancer is predominantly a disease of the city dweller lends "very serious support" to the theory that atmospheric pollution plays a predominant role.
"But I myself do not believe that cigarette smoking or atmospheric pollution as such cause cancer of the lung. My own feeling is that they probably determine the site at which the patient gets his cancer."
The Globe and Mail of January 17, 1955, carries a statement attributed to the noted German specialist and Nobel medicine prize winner, Dr. Otto Warburg:
Warburg, who won the Nobel prize for medicine in 1931, said he has established that lack of oxygen respiration of the body cells is a major cause of chronic damage to normal cells and their conversion into cancerous cells.

Warburg admits that lack of oxygen can by no means be regarded as the sole cause, "but intermittent lack of oxygen will be a frequent cause as, for instance, pressure on the blood vessels frequently results in the intermittent lack of oxygen in the body."
He suggests the following preventive measures: Do not inhale cigaret smoke; ban diesel oil fumes from the streets; forbid curing of foodstuffs with certain cures; ban the dyeing of foodstuffs with aniline dyes; forbid the preservation of foodstuffs with antiseptic substances.
The London Free Press of April 30, 1955, carried a report of an interview with Dr. William Franks. Dr. Franks was being questioned by Jacqueline Moore and in reply to the question, "What has our environment got to do with lung cancer?" he said:
The world is full of cancer-producing agents, or carcinogens, as we call them. Tar on asphalt highways, for instance, Nickel-carbonyl. Chromates. Fuel oil. Radioactive compounds. Even sunshine. An idling automobile engine. Rubber tires. A faulty oil furnace. Commercial soot. Even printers' ink. All these things are known to contain substances which can cause cancer experimentally. Inject the dust of any one of these products into a mouse and you'll be liable to get a tumor. Do you know that extracts of dust from the air of eight large American cities have been injected into mice and they developed cancer? Why put all the blame on cigarettes? The association between lung cancer and smoking is real enough, but it's not the sole cause; it's probably only the straw that broke the camel's back. It's our whole noxious environment. And that's why I say we can do something about lung cancer because we can clean up the air we breathe. We are at the stage now where we must pay as much attention to the air as we pay to our water supply.
And finally, Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote extracts from an article which appeared in the September 21, 1955, edition of the Ottawa Journal. This article concerns a report prepared by Dr. A. H. Sellers, a medical statistician of the Ontario department of health who appeared before the Ontario legislature select committee on air pollution and smoke control. The article says in part:
"There is seen to be some correlation between the respiratory cancer mortality for males and the proportion of the population residing in urban areas", the report said. "This correlation is not shown for females."
Deaths from cancer of the trachea, lungs and bronchus; from cancer of all forms and from pneumonia and bronchitis were unexpectedly low in the rural areas and municipalities with populations under 15,000.
The report said studies made elsewhere have shown that mortality from lung cancer in England, Wales and Denmark is higher in urban areas than in rural.
In England it appeared to be related to the density of buildings rather than that of population. Atmospheric pollution was increasing in England while lung cancer was rising.'
There is much more evidence I could give, Mr. Speaker, but I hesitate to take more time of the house when I believe all hon. members will agree that the problem is

serious enough to deserve action. The question is, "what can we do?"
For several years now diesel engines have been used underground in mining operations of various kinds. It would not have been possible, had they not devised an economical method of rendering these diesel fumes practically harmless, to miners working underground in contact with these fumes. The equipment used is known to the trade as a "scrubber". Briefly, it is an arrangement whereby the exhaust fumes are passed through an aqueous solution of sodium sulphite, with a percentage of hydroquinone added. The cost of chemicals for operating this device is in the neighbourhood of 10 cents per working hour. The cost of the equipment is not unreasonable, and I understand it is presently available.
How many hon. members have followed behind a diesel truck or bus on the highway for any distance? I'll wager that you either passed it as soon as possible or slowed up to let it get ahead far enough that the fumes did not bother you. True diesel trucks have an upright exhaust pipe, but it is useless on the highway travelling at the ordinary speed. The vacuum behind the truck sucks the exhaust fumes down to highway level and these fumes are taken into newer model cars via the front air vents. You can see proof of that from the fact that the tarpaulins on these diesel trucks are blackened right from the front to the back and down the back of the truck. Most motorists realize that these air vents should be closed when overtaking a diesel truck or bus on the highway or in heavy traffic, but how many bother to do so, until the odour becomes noticeable.
That may be good enough for diesel fumes but remember you cannot smell carbon monoxide. It is not only motorists who are subjected to these fumes. Pedestrians on city streets where diesel buses are used get a substantial amount every time a bus passes them. These fumes are quite noticeable also to passengers in buses, especially at stops when doors are opened. Most passengers on diesel powered trains have noticed the fumes when the air conditioning is turned on in their sleeping quarters. Almost everyone has noticed the irritating qualities of diesel exhaust fumes, but what do we do about it? Grumble, but accept it as part of present-day living until public opinion is aroused to the point where governments are forced into action.
I consider we have sufficient proof to suggest that diesel fumes are a contributing factor in the cause of lung cancer. Do we

have any proof that carbon monoxide poisoning is not the cause of many heart conditions? The finger of suspicion could definitely be pointed in that direction at least.
It is only fair for me to state at this time that the government is doing a limited amount of work on air pollution in the Department of National Health and Welfare under the directorship of Dr. Morris Katz. I sincerely suggest that much more could be done and that the government could set a good example by looking into the possibility of installing "scrubbers" on all the diesel locomotives on the Canadian National Railways system.
The danger is obvious. Action should be taken without further delay, and I hope hon. members from both sides of the house will support this resolution.

I may say that the researches and experiments being carried on in the United States, to a lesser extent in Great Britain and I understand also in Belgium and France, and before the war in Germany, have produced results which are familiar to the officers of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
As a matter of fact, for many years the Department of National Health and Welfare
and provincial and local authorities in Canada have carried out measures to safeguard human health by ensuring the safety and purity of drinking water, food and drugs and insecticides, and more particularly the air which we breathe has come under surveillance. The problem is one, not only of scientific interest but of the health of the people and it is well that from time to time when we spend so much time on other matters of a political character that we should accord an opportunity in this house for the discussion of matters as constructive as is this particular question.
Air pollution has been of course the inevitable accompaniment of industrialization and growth of our large cities. I may take as an example of what we have attempted in our department as the result of suggestions made by provincial governments and officials in the United States the researches that have been carried on in the Detroit-Windsor area. That area was chosen because that is the largest Canadian city on the Canadian side of the border close to a large United States community. This is an example of international co-operative effort to try to determine the extent of air pollution and the dire results that come from that kind of pollution.
In that area the Department of National Health and Welfare, in co-operation with the department of health of Ontario, the department of health of Detroit and the board of health of Windsor, have been carrying on for some time one of the most extensive investigations of the result of air pollution on human health which I think has ever been undertaken. That has been under way now for two years on both sides of the river involving a careful examination of family groups and individuals in an effort to ascertain the effect of air pollution conditions emanating particularly from the large industrial centre of Detroit and the large industrial centre of Canada's first city, the city of Windsor.

I appreciate that the house has recognized the high priority I have placed on the community which is mine. This pioneering effort and the results of this study undoubtedly will yield much information of value to health departments all over the world. An assessment of the study is now under way but it will be some time before all of the statistical data are finally determined. Undoubtedly it will play its part, as studies to which my hon. friend referred have played their part, in enabling him and others to formulate opinions on various aspects of this
670	HOUSE OF
Health-Poisonous Gases problem. It may be that with the information which this extensive air pollution study in the Detroit-Windsor area will yield it may be possible to provide for considerable improvement and amelioration.
The subject matter of the resolution of course relates to one aspect only of the overall problem of air pollution. Our officers have carefully studied all the implications of the resolution and I am bound to say that there is no doubt in their judgment that the operation of diesel vehicles in certain situations, especially in mining operations, in tunnels, and in more or less confined spaces, does represent a potential danger to health. We have placed the skill of the people in our occupational health division at the service of provincial departments who admittedly accept this as their primary constitutional responsibility. However, that does not deter us in any way from seeking to assist them in a matter which is of concern.
The control of this hazard in such cases is usually achieved, I am told, by the installation of adequate ventilation facilities. In the stationary type of engine the exhaust gases must be removed by piping into proper exhaust gas ventilators or ducts for disposal of the fumes. I am further advised that the operation of such vehicles or engines in the open atmosphere may constitute a hazard to health in areas of dense traffic and population. It may be that when the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hosking) was speaking of Guelph he was not speaking of an area of dense traffic and population.
This phase of the problem is now under intensive investigation, as my hon. friend has noted, in the area of Los Angeles, California, and a special study is under way by the automotive industry primarily in the city of Detroit. Waste products of internal combustion engines include unburned fuel or hydrocarbons, carbon monoxide, aldehydes, oxides of nitrogen, as well as carbon, soot, tarry material and other products, including water vapour. After listening to my dissertation-my hon. friend is smiling. I am sure that after listening to my dissertation he appreciates that he and I at least have one thing in common, that is the technical knowledge that each of us possesses in this important matter.
I am told that the theory has been postulated in the Los Angeles area that smog is formed to a major degree by the interaction of such hydrocarbon waste products with oxides of nitrogen in the presence of oxygen and sunlight. Such chemical interactions of pollutants may be related to eye irritation and other health effects that have been


observed and to some of the crop damage sustained in the Los Angeles area. Perhaps it was this circumstance that brought my hon. friend to take an interest in this matter. In any event, that seems to be one of the implications involved. It is stated that, in the immediate vicinity of diesel engine exhaust, the concentrations of aldehydes and oxides of nitrogen may be sufficient to produce considerable eye, nose and throat irritation. I may say in this connection that Dr. Grove of our blindness control division has done considerable work in this particular field. I am sure the hon. gentleman would profit greatly if at his convenience some time he allowed me to arrange for him to discuss this matter with this outstanding public servant.
Various control methods have been suggested for reducing the toxicity of waste gases from internal combustion engines. These include systems for treating exhaust gases such as catalytic exhaust converters, after-burners, absorbers, condensers and filters.
Other proposals concern systems which modify engine operating conditions, such as manifold vacuum control, deceleration fuel cut-off, ignition timing control, recycling of exhaust gases and fuel injection. I simply add this rider, that objectionable visible smoke and fumes may be reduced greatly, my officers tell me, by improved maintenance practices. It may be that if greater care on the part of those who have the legal power to require enforcement were taken to see that this enforcement took place, many of the abuses to which my hon. friend has directed our attention could be avoided.
I can point out that there are now under investigation by the automobile industry such proposals as the change in the design of cylinder combustion chambers, carburetors and intake manifolds.
It has been shown in field and laboratory tests by the Los Angeles air pollution control authority that approximately seven per cent of all fuels used by automobiles is discharged unburned into the atmosphere, and this constitutes the greatest single source of hydrocarbon loss in the Los Angeles area. However, I am advised by my technical officers that no success has yet beeen achieved in securing the development of a control device suitable for controlling the emissions of exhaust gases from automobiles.
In the case of diesel engines, a limited amount of control has been achieved with the installation of exhaust gas absorbers which contain alkaline and other types of solutions for removal of aldehydes and oxides of nitrogen.

Health-Poisonous Gases
Several companies in the United States, including the Houdry Corporation and the Catalytic Combustion Corporation, are experimenting with catalytic systems for more complete combustion of exhaust gases and also with various types of after-burners. This work, however, is still, I am advised, in the development stage.
Much more study and research is needed before adequate means are available for the control of emissions from trucks, tractors, buses and other types of vehicles on highways and railways, apart from the abatement of smoke and visible exhaust fumes by proper maintenance practices.
I would tell my hon. friend and the house that the development of effective controls for exhaust gas waste products is contingent upon the successful completion of studies that are now in progress, some in this country but a great many in the United States. As I have already noted in respect of one aspect of the problem, we have undertaken in Canada in co-operation with the city of Detroit a most extensive study.
At the end of his speech the hon. gentleman mentioned that for a very small amount of money a device could be used which would avoid the dangers feared. I was not aware of that device and I asked my parliamentary assistant to contact the officers of our department. They advise me that, with regard to scrubbers for diesel engines, these scrubbers contain water to which are added alkalis, ferrous sulphate or other ingredients which remove the aldehydes and to a certain extent the oxides of nitrogen. Our officers tell us that these are not very effective for carbon monoxide, and that therefore adequate ventilation is still required. Their value has not been proven for railways or diesel transport trucks on highways, but there are three places where these particular devices are now being subjected to strict study and scrutiny, and it may be that we shall have more information on which to pass a final judgment.
Before taking my seat, I should like to mention that the hon. gentleman referred to cancer and the studies which I announced in this house, regarding one alleged form of cancer. Those studies are now under way, as a result of the financial contributions made by one company in addition to the grants that have been accorded by the federal government.
As the hon. gentleman mentioned, Dr. Warwick, the director of the institute, has made mention of some of these researches. I forget whether my hon. friend did go on to say, but Dr. Warwick could have gone on to say, that, as a result of funds which this
parliament had voted, researches are now under way in at least two different universities in Canada in the matter of analysing the possible potential relation between some of the factors of causation of cancer mentioned by my hon. friend. In any event, I hope I have indicated to my hon. friend that these matters are the subject of research by those who are qualified to engage in this kind of examination.
My hon. friend may well feel he has served a useful purpose in bringing this matter to the attention of the public. He may be assured that, to the extent that this is a matter within our competence, it will continue to have our sustained interest and, to the extent that we can assist the provincial governments in the prosecution of this matter, this will be done. With that in view, I am sure my hon. friend would agree that this would possibly be the appropriate moment to withdraw his motion.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO MEDICAL EXPENSES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation amending the Income Tax Act so as to remove therefrom the 3 per cent floor in relation to the deductibility of medical expenses for income tax purposes.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion makes a request, the subject matter of which is well known to hon. members of this house and is well known throughout the country. It

asks that what is known as the 3 per cent floor in relation to the deductibility of medical expenses for income tax purposes be removed and that medical expenses be allowed deductibility right from the first dollar.
Last year when I moved a motion in terms identical with this one the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benidickson) was gracious enough to say some kind words about the fact that I had added some new arguments and some new material to my speech of the previous year. I am sorry to disappoint him but so far as this year is concerned it is not I who will be introducing the new material. I hope that the "something new" will come from the government side of the house.
I think it is time the government took this matter seriously. I think it is time the government realized the feeling of the Canadian people that this request . is a just one. I think it is time the government took the action proposed in this motion and removed the 3 per cent floor.
Hon. members are aware that this matter has been discussed in the house for quite a number of years. It was discussed generally in the debate on the speech from the throne, in the budget debate, and so on, in the late forties and early fifties. In 1951 it was the subject of a motion which I presented to the house but it was defeated. Again in 1952 it was the subject of a motion in my name and on that occasion the motion carried. It was passed unanimously by the house and the house thereby called upon the government to consider the advisability of removing what was then the 4 per cent floor. The house, and I think I can say the country as a whole, was disappointed when the consideration which we can only assume was given by the government to this matter resulted in no action at that session of parliament.
The next year, 1953, I again brought in the motion. On that occasion only two speeches were made; mine and that of the then minister of finance, Mr. Abbott, who at the conclusion of his speech moved that the debate be adjourned so that there was no further discussion on the motion at that point. However, when Mr. Abbott brought down his budget of 1953-which, of course, we cannot but remember was in an election year-he at least took the action of reducing the 4 per cent floor to the present level of 3 per cent. Well, that was a step in the right direction which was appreciated. One remembers that when medical expense deductibility was first provided for in 1942 and 1943 the floor was at 5 per cent, so we are glad to note that the floor is gradually

being lowered, first from 5 to 4 per cent in 1944 and then in 1953 from 4 to 3 per cent.
But as one who feels it should be abolished altogether I did not allow the matter to rest on the basis of the action taken in 1953 but I again brought in the motion in 1954, asking at that time that the then 3 per cent floor be wiped out. That motion was again defeated. Last year I brought in the motion again, and again it was defeated. But last year the margin of defeat was not very great considering the tremendous superiority of the government strength in this house. The vote last year was only 86 to 60 against my motion.
Well, it is now before the house again. In the meantime hon. members have had an opportunity to think more about it and to sense the feelings of their constituents back home in relation to the subject and I hope on this occasion there will be a more favourable result than in the past few years.
I confess, Mr. Speaker, that I had dared to hope that other developments might make unnecessary a motion of this kind at this time. I shall refer very briefly to these other developments which I hoped might take place. We knew there was to be a meeting of the federal government with the provincial governments on health insurance and I dared to hope that the results of that meeting might be sufficiently far-reaching that individual medical expenses might be cut down to the point where a matter of this kind would not be of such importance as it has been in the past.
However, despite the fact that one welcomes the steps that have been taken in the right direction by the conference which met last week, it still remains clear that even if the proposals of the federal government are accepted by a sufficient number of provinces and come into effect, there still remains a great area of medical expenses, particularly doctors' bills and dental bills, as well as many other kinds of medical expenses, which will have to be met by individual Canadians. Therefore the problem of the impact of individual medical expenses, although it will be ameliorated slightly if the government's proposals with regard to hospitalization and other services come into effect, will still remain for the great bulk of our Canadian citizens. Hence I once again present this motion, Mr. Speaker, so the government might have this opportunity to show that it is really concerned for the health of the Canadian people, and might show that concern in this small way by permitting the deductibility of medical expenses right from the first dollar.
As hon. members are aware, the right to deduct one's medical expenses is surrounded by certain limitations. For example, there is an absolute ceiling as to the amount one
Income Tax Act
can claim as a deduction. That ceiling is at the figure of $1,500 for a single taxpayer and $2,000 for a married taxpayer plus $500 for each dependent up to a limit of $2,000 for dependents. That is one of the limitations on the deduction of medical expenses. You cannot deduct them all. You can deduct them only up to a certain point. Another of the limitations is that only certain prescribed kinds of expense can be deducted. You can deduct what you pay to a hospital; you can deduct doctors' bills, dentists' bills, nurses' bills and so on. You can deduct the costs of a few drugs which have been put on the list, and certain other specified expenses.
The fact is, however, that there are a great many expenses which are really medical or which relate to illness but which you are not permitted to deduct. There is, of course, the question of spectacles and devices of that kind. Most drugs and medicines are still not on the list of expenses that you can deduct for income tax purposes. Then, of course, there is the whole problem of help in the home that may be required at the time of illness, and all sorts of other expenses with which one is faced when illness strikes.
The other day I drew to the attention of the house that strange case-something that seems to be most unfair-in which a taxpayer was denied the right to charge as a medical expense the sum of over $700 which he had had to pay for oxygen in order to keep alive his wife who was suffering from tuberculosis. The reason given by the income tax branch and accepted by the income tax appeal board for refusing to allow that expense was that it was not paid directly to a hospital or a medical institution as defined in the act.
I mention that matter in passing, expressing the hope that the situation will be corrected in the budget this year. I mention it also to indicate that there are many items which are not allowed as medical expenses. Therefore the words which appear in the income tax form, and which make it clear to the taxpayer that he cannot deduct all his medical expenses, are indeed quite correct.
Those are two of the limitations, namely the ceiling and the limited list of things that you can deduct. The third limitation is this 3 per cent floor which is the subject matter of my resolution. I have made it clear before, and I do so again, that I have no quarrel with the ceiling. The figures which set the ceiling are reasonably ample, it seems to me. However, I do have a quarrel with the limited nature of the list of items that can be charged as medical expenses. I feel that that list should be extended. At any rate, I have not confused the issue by putting

Income Tax Act
that question into my resolution. I have confined my resolution to the one question, namely that the 3 per cent floor should be abolished.
Even at the expense of repeating what has been said just about every time this matter has come before the house, let me take a moment to remind hon. members that when you set about to deduct medical expenses from your income tax, you first of all must strike a figure that is 3 per cent of your net income. For all practical purposes your net income is just about your total income; at least it is closer to your total income than it is to your taxable income. Net income is the gross income you receive less one or two specific deductions, such as pension fund deductions, deductions for trade union dues and so on. That figure to which you must apply the 3 per cent is the figure you have before you deduct the $1,000 or $2,000 statutory exemption, or whatever your exemption may be. Hence if you are a person with an income of $3,000 a year, the first $90 of your medical expenses are not allowed as deductible. If your medical expenses in a year are $75 or $30, you get no credit for them. If your medical expenses are $100, you get credit for $10, namely the amount over the $90 figure which represents the application of the 3 per cent floor.
I have repeated that again despite the fact that it is well known to all of us and to most people in this country. My reason for doing so is to make clear what it is that we are asking for. In the example I gave of a taxpayer with a $3,000 income and having $100 medical expenses in a year, we are asking that he should be allowed to deduct from his taxable income not just the $10 that he is allowed at the present time but the full $100 of those medical expenses.
As I have pointed out on six or eight occasions now, it is a fact that if one makes contributions to approved charities he is allowed to deduct those contributions from his taxable income; and although there is a ceiling, as there is with respect to medical expenses, still there is no floor. You are allowed to deduct charitable donations right from the first dollar. If a person is allowed to deduct charitable donations, which are voluntary, right from the first dollar, we feel strongly that the same privilege should be accorded to taxpayers with regard to medical expenses, which are certainly involuntary.
In the past I have given various examples, and I think perhaps I should give them again if for no other reason than to put the matter in terms of the income tax rates that apply for the present year. I take in the first place
[Mr. Knowles.l
the example of a married taxpayer with no children, and having an income of $2,400 a year. That taxpayer's income tax, including his old age security tax, would amount to $60. If that person had medical expenses of $200 in a year his tax would be reduced to $40.80, or he would get a tax rebate or tax credit of $19.20. But if that same person, instead of having- to spend $200 on medical expenses, were to give $200 to an approved charity, his tax would be reduced to $30. In other words his saving would be $30. It is that discrepancy, that difference, that we think is unfair. We think the person who is allowed $30 in tax rebate for giving away $200 to charity should be allowed the same amount if he has to spend that much on medical expenses.
I come to the example of a married couple having two children of family allowance age. Let us assume that their income is $3,600 a year. Under this year's rates their total income tax before any other adjustments would be $201. If this family had medical expenses of $300 in a year their income tax would be reduced to $168.36, leaving a tax saving of $32.64. But if that same family, instead of spending $300 involuntarily on medical expenses, were to give away $300 to approved charities their income tax would be reduced to $150, making a saving of $51. Putting the two side by side, their income tax saving for $300 given to charity is $51, but their income tax saving for $300 medical expenses is only $32.64. We think the two should be put on the same footing.
My next example is that of a married taxpayer having two children of family allowance age where the total income is $5,000 a year. Their income tax before any adjustment would be $453. If this family has medical expenses of $500 their income tax will be reduced to $386.50, representing a saving of $66.50. If this family gives the same amount, namely $500, to an approved charity, their tax [DOT]is reduced to $358, so that the saving is $95. The tax saving for $500 of medical expenses is $66.50, but the tax saving for $500 given to charity is $95.
I move back again into the lower income brackets. I cite the case of a married taxpayer with two children of family allowance age trying to get by in this day and age on $2,400 a year. Their tax before any adjustments would be only $15 for 1956, according to the law as it now stands. If they have medical expenses of $100 their tax will be $10.80, representing a saving of $4.20. But if they give away $100-don't ask me how anybody earning $2,400 and supporting a wife and two children could give away $100-the entire $15 income tax would be wiped out.

There would be a saving of $15 that way, but there would be a saving of only $4.20 if the family has $100 of medical expenses.
Let me take just one more of these examples. As the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance will probably notice, these are the same examples I used last year, except that I have worked them out in terms of the income tax rates that are now provided in the Income Tax Act. My last case, therefore, is that of a married taxpayer with two children of family allowance age where the income is $3,000 a year. The tax before any adjustment would be $105. If this family had $100 of medical expenses, their tax would be reduced to $103.50, a reduction of $1.50. But if the same family gave away $100 their tax would be reduced to $90, or a saving of $15.
I have given a great many figures in the last few minutes. Let me put these last two alongside each other. In that last example, the income tax saving for $100 of medical expenses is $1.50, but the income tax saving for $100 given to charity is $15 or ten times as much. We feel this year, as we felt last year, the year before that and the year before that back until we first started this campaign, that it is not fair to continue that discrepancy. We feel that the same treatment should be accorded to those two types of expenses or contributions.
There have been times when it has been suggested to me that this would be a great boon to the wealthy, more of a boon to the wealthy than it would be to those in the lower brackets. The fact of the matter is that our concern is for the little people, for those who just do not get into this bracket because their expenses are not over the 3 per cent level. Actually, if you want to talk about the very wealthy, the ceiling which the government has imposed would prevent any great bonanza coming to them as a result of the removal of the floor. For example, if a person had an income of $20,000, at the present time he would get only the portion of those expenses in excess of $600, which is 3 per cent of the $20,000, and even that would be limited by the ceiling. If such a person were married and had $3,000 of medical expenses he would not be allowed the whole $3,000. He would not even get the $2,400 which is over the $600 floor. He would have only $2,000 allowed as deductible because of the ceiling which is there. That is one of the reasons I do not object to the ceiling, because if you take away the floor you find in the example I have just given that $2,000 is the maximum the wealthy person can claim. In an outlandish case such as that-or go higher 67509-43J
Income Tax Act
if you will, to persons with incomes up to $50,000 or $100,000-in most cases you are not going to get any tax relief from the removal of the floor, because of the ceiling. Indeed, the government raised the ceiling a bit in 1952, the year in which we thought we had won the battle for the abolition of what was then the 4 per cent floor.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as hon. members are aware I am rather full of this subject, having spoken on it so often. But as I indicated in my opening remarks the new thing that is needed, the something new that should be added, is not additional argument from this side of the house. The something new that should be added is an awareness on the part of the government that the time has come for favourable action on this matter. I am grateful for the support we have received in the past from members of the opposition in whatever part of the house they sit. They have supported this matter every time I have raised it. I am grateful for the unanimous support given to my motion in 1952. I am grateful also for the support that was given by a few Liberals, even in years when the measure was not looked upon with too much favour from the government side of the house.
I recall the supporting remarks of the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Henry) and the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier). I recall also the approval of the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Maltais). I recall the interest in this matter of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite) and his implied support of the proposal. I remember, too, that long ago there were requests for the extension of this principle by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) and even by the present Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) when he was the more humble private member for Renfrew South. I am grateful also for the support that has been given in the past by one who is no longer with us, one who has gone to his reward in the other place, the former member for Spadina.
It is perhaps unfair to single out only half a dozen Liberals when there have been 60 or more on the opposition side of the house who have stood up for this proposition every time it has been raised. And yet perhaps it is significant that there were six or eight on the other side of the house who felt that a few words might be spoken in favour of this principle of extending the coverage of income deductibility, no matter what stand the government was taking.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I want to see the list of allowable expenses extended.

Income Tax Act
I am also interested in a resolution on the order paper in the name of an hon. member from my own city. I may not agree with all its details, but I am interested in the proposal that premiums and taxes paid for hospitalization plans and health insurance schemes might be included as well. There is a whole range of things that might be discussed, but it seems to me the most important thing is to get rid of this floor and permit taxpayers to deduct their medical expenses right from the first dollar.
There is wide public interest in this. No one contributed more to the widening of that interest than did the former minister of finance in 1952 by taking a negative view on the matter, after the decision of the house that the government should consider the advisability of removing the floor. I thank him for the attention he drew to it in that way. I call on the present government and the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) to look on this matter favourably, to consider the justice of our appeal and to take action at this session to remove this floor. Toward that end I hope the house will support the motion which I now have the honour to present.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO MEDICAL EXPENSES
speechtext:
Those who were in the house in 1952 will well recall what happened when a similar motion dealing with a 4 per cent figure was introduced by the hon. member who has introduced this motion today. Everyone in the house appeared to give approval to the resolution at that time and undoubtedly all, with the exception apparently of those who sat on the treasury benches, expected the government to give some regard or effect to the resolution on which the house had so strongly declared itself. But we had assumed that there was more responsible government in the chamber than proved to be the fact; for the Minister of Finance did not choose to be bound by the firm and unanimous declaration of the opinion of the house.
However, before the last election the Minister of Finance did bring in a budget proposal which, so far as it went, did receive the unanimous approval of the house, contemplating a reduction from 4 per cent to 3 per cent of that portion of taxable income which must be first subtracted before medical expenses can be deducted in determining taxable income.
The Conservatives in the house, Mr. Speaker, have supported this resolution in the past and will, I am sure, continue to do so. It seems to me there is every reason why, in looking for means of introducing more

equity into our taxation laws, as well as seeking needed reductions in taxation, this particular proposal should be favoured as one entitled to high priority.
It is not to be overlooked that the cost of hospitalization and medical expense is rising substantially all the time. On some other occasion we shall no doubt hear a good deal about the very heavy burden that is borne by the Canadian people in respect of their outlays on hospital, medical and nursing expenditures. It seems to me that this type of expenditure is a very proper one to be favoured from the point of view of deductions that ought to be fallowed to taxpayers in calculating their taxable income.
Sir, I do not propose to discuss this matter at length. There is a question of principle involved here. I suppose we can expect to hear from the government the familiar refrain that it is estimated, based upon statistical reviews, that an average of 4 per cent of the income of the people goes to pay medical, hospital and nursing expenses, and therefore it is fair enough that that percentage should be subtracted, or a similar proportion should be subtracted, in reckoning what should be allowed by way of deduction on this account from income.
Well, sir, these statistics can be used to deal with average expenditure, but in my view average expenditure is not sufficient to justify any further withholding by the government of this benefit from the taxpayers. There are very good reasons why we should go the whole way and eliminate the 3 per cent which is now subtracted. The burden is never equally distributed; the outlays on medical and hospital expenses fall disproportionately heavily on those of modest income, but it affects all and here is a good place to bring a general benefit to bear for all taxpayers.
Hon. members who have followed debates on this subject in the past will not be surprised if I advert to a subject on which I have addressed the house on many occasions, namely the altogether too narrow definition that is placed by the act and by the government in its administration of the act on medical expenses. We have had many debates on this subject. Attention has been drawn repeatedly to the fact that some extraordinary anomalies exist under the present act, and those anomalies have not been improved by the way in which the act has been administered by the government.
Why some appliances prescribed, for example, by physicians should be regarded as proper medical expenses and others disallowed is something I have never been able to justify on any basis of logic. We have

the familiar example of spectacles. They are not permitted to be included in the medical expenses of the taxpayer. Why they should not I have never been able to understand. The act permits certain forms of hearing aids to be included in the category, but aids to vision are rejected. One could go down through the category of appliances as defined in the act or in the light of the interpretations put upon the provisions of the act in the administration thereof.
Then there is the matter of drugs. This is a subject again that has engaged the attention of the house frequently, and where some remedial legislation is badly needed. The act has been amended on a couple of occasions in recent years specifically to permit about four drugs to be treated as deductible, in other words entitled to be included in the list of medical expenses. But why some should be included and others rejected again defies any sense of logic, and in many respects a sense of fair play. Sir, if drugs are prescribed by physicians as required for the health of a patient, why should they not be regarded as medical expenses?
Then we have a further anomaly, sir, in the case of physicians doing their own dispensing. Apart from four named drugs in the act, no status whatever is given to expenditures on drugs, even though prescribed by physicians, so far as the definition of medical expenses is concerned. We know that physicians in the cities and towns normally do not do their own dispensing. The country physician almost of necessity must do his own dispensing, and when he includes drugs or medicines in an allinclusive account to the patient those items are allowed by the government. This anomaly has been known to exist for years, but the government has taken no remedial action as yet.
I am glad this motion offers an opportunity to reaffirm the support which has been given on previous occasions to the purport and principle of this resolution, and to point out that anomalies continue to exist and that the government has failed repeatedly to bring forward proposals at budget time designed to cope with these existing anomalies. Surely the time has come when this matter can no longer escape the attention of the government.

Mr. Speaker, I find myself in agreement with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). As the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) has said, many of us have expressed our approval in the past. As has been stated this afternoon, the resolution
Income Tax Act moved by the hon. member has had our support on other occasions, and in fact on one occasion it had the support of the whole house.
I never could understand why the government has not taken more action than they have on this resolution. It has met with unusual unanimity, because we all agree that the fear of medical expenses is one of the greatest fears that a family man and his wife can have; especially those, such as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre mentioned, who find difficulty in getting along on the wages they are earning.
That has been recognized no doubt by the whole house, in fact even by the government and the cabinet which refused to accept the unanimous recommendation of the house. Recently this government has been discussing health insurance policies with the provinces. That matter has been recognized by the party supporting the government for well over a quarter of a century because they have played with the idea at every election they have held for almost a third of a century.
It seems to me that principle has not been followed in practice. In fact one might take advantage of this opportunity to suggest to the government that before the budget is brought down they give consideration to going beyond this 3 per cent exemption and allowing contributions made by those who assist in the payment of medical expenses incurred by patients who cannot afford to pay them. I know of some hon. members who have been in near financial embarrassment for many years because they have taken care of members of their families over long periods of illness.
Those who contribute to the building of a hospital or who make substantial gifts to a hospital are allowed to deduct those contributions from income for income tax purposes under the present regulations. On the other hand, if a person contributes toward the care of a patient in hospital I think he should be entitled to a similar exemption.
I am not going to burden the house by repeating what has been said in other years or what has been said so well by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, except to say that it seems to me the government somewhat accepted the principle when they reduced the floor from 4 per cent to 3 per cent just before the last election. I would certainly be sorry to see this government remain in power long enough for them to have a sufficient number of elections to get the other 3 per cent off, because it would appear that it would take quite a long time even if they accepted the principle since

Income Tax Act
apparently they take off only 1 per cent at a time. I do not know why they did not take off the 3 per cent because, as has been mentioned by the mover of the resolution, it means that the man with a small income does not receive much benefit while the man with a larger income, who usually does not find medical expenses too great a burden, is allowed to deduct what he pays out for medical expenses, what he pays to the hospital or for other charitable services.
I would urge the government to take cognizance of the motion before the house. Before the budget is brought down I hope the government and the cabinet will consider the approval that has been given to this matter, especially the complete unanimity which was shown in 1952. I expect that it will all disappear if we should have an election in 1956, or at least a portion of it; but even if we do not have an election until 1957 I would urge the government to adopt the principle and not wait to remove 1 per cent at election time, but remove the 3 per cent even a year before the election.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am completely in support of the resolution. It must be borne in mind that what is paid out for medical expenses is a dead loss. Usually a person faced with the payment of medical expenses also has his earning capacity decreased to a considerable degree. Frequently the total cost of a sickness cannot appear in any record which a person might present to show that he has been faced with medical expenses. For example, different kinds of food may have to be provided in nursing an individual back to health. There are many other ways in which the account presented by a doctor or hospital would not show the total cost.
