speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO MEDICAL EXPENSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the sponsor of this resolution has said, we have had a discussion on this matter during each of the past several years. The records of Hansard are available to indicate the general principles which the government has advanced in debating this question from year to year.
I would remind hon. members that this particular exemption is of rather short-term duration in our income tax law. It was introduced as an exception to the general principles in 1942, and I think for a good reason. At that time, because of the war, the tax rates were at a very high level indeed. I could illustrate by simply pointing out that

in the case of a married man without dependents with an income of $2,500, the tax and compulsory savings amounted to $651. At that time it was recognized, fortunately that a taxpayer who had extraordinarily high medical expenses would be in a very difficult position indeed, in view of the portion of his income that was required to finance the conflict in which we were then engaged. In the case of a married man without dependents with an income of $3,000, the tax and compulsory savings taken from him for the requirements of the government in 1942 amounted to $384.
In consequence there was a departure from the basic principle that there is one over-all personal exemption applying to the normal cost of living of all citizens. I may say that under our Canadian taxation provisions, that basic personal allowance and deduction from gross income before taxes are imposed is a larger sum than in either the United States or Great Britain, or indeed in any comparable country that we could consider in connection witht modern tax provisions.
I should like to point out that in recent years there has been a very substantial decrease in the general income tax that applies to people in the income groups I have already mentioned. As I have said, we have had debates on this subject in each of the past several years. I have indicated in debates in former years that the actual cost to the treasury of acceding to this form of tax relief would be in the neighbourhood of $50 million or $60 million. When tax reductions are possible, one must consider what form of tax relief would provide the widest possible benefit and would have the best possible economic results.
We had a very substantial tax reduction in 1953 as compared with 1952. I want to point out that an individual, married and with two dependents, respecting 1952 income was paying an income tax of $88. That was reduced in 1953, and it was reduced again last year. The same is true of the other person I used as an illustration, namely a married man earning $3,000, who in 1952 was paying a tax of $175 and in 1956 will pay a tax of $130. I point out to hon. members that this means broadly a reduction of 25 per cent in those years. That tax reduction applies to all taxpayers, whether or not they have had the particular misfortune of having medical bills to pay.
I also say that this form of utilization of tax deduction possibilities has considerable merit, because a great proportion of the working force of this country are not in the income tax paying group at all. To use

approximate figures, we could say that the working force of this country is probably of the size of about five and a half million people. Some two million in that group do not at the present time have to pay income tax, because of the general exemptions that are provided in our law. It would be obvious to members that the form of tax relief suggested by the sponsor of this motion would apply only to persons who are in the smaller income taxpaying group.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said he hoped there would be some new note in the annual debate on this subject. It must be obvious to him that one of the outstanding new notes that could be referred to would be the very important events of last week when the federal government, in the health field, made propositions to the provinces for sharing costs of hospital and diagnostic health services to a very impressive, and indeed gigantic, extent. The implications of that offer, if the majority of the provinces see fit to accept it, are at the present time, in dollar value, probably of the order of four or five times what is involved in this particular form of approach to the health question.
I would point out in connection with my other remarks that this form of federal government participation in the health field would be of general application, contrary to a scheme such as is proposed, which would assist with respect to health problems only those citizens who are in the income taxpaying group.
I would also remind hon. members, as we are inclined to forget, that actual individual tax rates have dropped radically from 1942, when I indicated the very great proportion of the income of one in the lower brackets-or in any bracket-that was required for governmental purposes. Indeed, I pointed out that the reduction in the tax rate for a person earning $3,000 is from $884 in 1942 to $130 in 1956.
In connection with the opportunities for tax deductions in this particular field for health expenses, the law has been very radically liberalized since 1942. In 1942 the ceiling of the total medical expenses that would be considered for exemption for tax purposes was only a fraction of what is provided for at the present time. In most of the years since 1945 there have been added other provisions that are greatly to the advantage of the taxpayer. The types of drugs, types of appliances and the calendar period for consideration have all been changed very greatly to the advantage of the taxpayer.
These details have all been set out in past debates but I would not want hon. members
Income Tax Act
to overlook them. In addition there have been two changes in the rate of percentage for medical expense deduction that is considered as the norm, or the rate which must be exceeded if one is to get consideration for tax relief in this field. Originally it was 5 per cent. It was reduced in 1944 to 4 per cent. The hon. members who have spoken thus far have overlooked what was announced as the reason for that reduction from 5 per cent to 4 per cent.
The main reason for that reduction was a recognition of the fact, as was pointed out at that time, that the administrative cost of examining the number of small drug accounts that might be submitted by a taxpayer would be exceedingly expensive to the crown in the matter of administration. So in a general way the rate was reduced from 4 per cent to 3 per cent, taking that into account. Certain exceptionally expensive drugs were in themselves given qualification for exemption under the income tax statute as well.
Some reference has been made to a recent appeal under the Income Tax Act with respect to the expense of purchasing oxygen. As a matter of fact, although every year individuals, members of parliament, sometimes officers of the Department of National Health and Welfare and other people prior to the consideration of the annual budget present recommendations to the finance minister concerning things which they think should be subject to consideration in this section of the Income Tax Act. It happens the matter of oxygen is not one of those items which has been directed particularly to the attention of the department for tax consideration.
This section of the Income Tax Act receives very careful attention each year from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) and all the officials of his department as well as the Department of National Revenue. All the recommendations that have been received in the preceding year from hon. members of this house and from outside the house are most carefully studied. It is a practice to seek the advice of the Department of National Health and Welfare in regard to the relative costliness, the apparent worth and necessity, and some other factors relating to a particular drug. I assure hon. members, several of whom have made some representation urging the addition of certain specific drugs beyond those which have been considered for exemption, that this aspect will be reviewed again in the weeks that are to ensue prior to the bringing down of the new budget.
I should like to point out that under present tax law a person married, without dependents, with an income of $3,000 whose medical expenses would be totally exempt under this

Income Tax Act
motion, would receive a tax benefit of $13.50. I have no doubt whatever that most of the people across the country who read the newspapers and learn that this parliament is considering the question of deducting all medical expenses without any limitations such as we now have, at the 3 per cent level, will think that what is being considered is a deduction of the medical expenses from the amount of the tax cheque which they would otherwise be obliged to pay.
As I have pointed out, if the income of a married person were $3,000 the benefit under this resolution would be $13.50. This benefit would apply in a rather scattered form only to taxpayers who had to meet a particular medical situation. It would not have the merit of universality. In connection with the figure of $13.50 I would also like to point out that the tax reductions announced by the finance minister last year took no account of the previous tax reductions and provided tax relief for the person, married without dependents, earning $3,000 a year-comparing 1956 with 1954-to the extent of $20, compared with $13.50. That tax relief was available to everybody, and was available without the expense to the crown of examining every particular item of medical expense in the vouchers that would naturally end up with the examining officials in tremendous volume.
I think hon. members are fully aware, Mr. Speaker, of the basic principle that guides anyone when considering most carefully introducing into the Income Tax Act a very special feature that would exempt each and every form of medical expenditure. I mentioned that alternatively we have always placed general reliance on the basic personal exemption. What is allowed in this particular exemption is something that is considered unusual.
If every dollar of medical expense, dental expense and expenditures for drugs is to be allowed to the fullest extent as an exemption from gross income, and if those expenditures are of a normal nature and not of an unusual or hardship nature, I would ask hon. members what is the difference between allowing those and the suggestion that everyone should be entitled to put forward in detail the personal expenditure for clothes to keep one's family warm, the analogous expenditures on clothing or milk, food and the other necessities which constitute the normal expenditures of the average taxpayer.
In addition to that, although I deny that there is any failure to recognize in the health field the other difficulties which are encountered by taxpayers, I would point out there are also other hazards which sometimes provide unusual hardship. I could mention losses by taxpayers from fires, floods, tornadoes and

things of that kind. Contrary to what is done in the health field, there is no income tax recognition of these forms of personal catastrophe and unusual personal expense.
I repeat that we generally consider that it is a simplification and it is orderly to concentrate for tax purposes on a basic exemption. I repeat that in this country that basic exemption is more generous to the taxpayer than is available in almost any country with which I am familiar, and certainly in any that could be compared with Canada in its economic life.
As has been said in past years, apart from the decision the house may take on this motion this particular question is bound to be considered by all those who are giving attention to the budget in the ensuing weeks. Hon. members have made reference to a development in 1952 in this house when there was a concentration of attention on the word "consideration" contained in a similar resolution and when the former parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance said that as it was customary to consider each and every representation from all over the country prior to the presentation of the budget, he felt it was difficult to say that a House of Commons resolution stating that the house would like consideration to be given to a matter of this kind would be turned down by a majority vote.
Hon. members know it was made perfectly clear at that time that consideration would be given to the problem. Consideration was given to it. The then minister of finance and the parliamentary assistant, in subsequent speeches in this house, made that perfectly clear. But at the time the resolution was being considered those sponsoring it were emphasizing the word "consider" and the word "favourably" was not in the resolution. I remind hon. members that on many occasions subsequently opposition members have made reference to that result.
Despite the fact that consideration had been given as the minister assured the house it would be given, just because it was not consideration that resulted in a decision which the sponsor hoped for, I recall that the leader of the sponsor's party felt that he was justified in moving a vote of want of confidence in the government. As I say, on many occasions this matter has been referred to.
There is a difficulty in which hon. members are placed at the moment, particularly those who support the government. This resolution in its broad terms and representations concerns individual items of drugs and other liberalizations of the section which will be receiving attention. If hon. members were

to review the history of resolutions of this kind I think they will agree with me in this statement. I have no doubt that if the final result as announced in the budget was not completely to their satisfaction, they would have a great deal to say about the lack of consideration shown by the government, and what they might even think was some form of indifference to or lack of consideration for this house. I point out that fact to all hon. members.
I think it has been traditional that British parliaments do not consider that collectively they are in a position to move resolutions that affect the balance of ways and means. If hon. members, in advancing a motion of this kind, feel that it is obligatory for the government to accept the resolution fully, may I say this. I have indicated that it involves a revenue loss of $50 million. If this form of tax relief is given in this field, hon. members will realize the simplicity of the statement that it might deny relief in another field. Last year and in previous years I indicated what I thought were better forms of tax relief, provided on a better basis.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall make my remarks as brief as I can, so that if your decision on the yeas and the nays is not in the affirmative and a vote must be taken, we shall not have to take up too much of the supper hour.
The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance has once again given us a review of the government's position with respect to this matter, and he has tried once again to set out the government's defence for not yet having removed the floor with regard to medical expenses. He started off by reminding us that this form of tax relief was first introduced in 1942, becoming fully effective in 1943, because of the abnormally high taxes which were in effect at that time. He makes a great deal out of the fact that income taxes have gone down considerably since then. He is correct in that statement. However, what he overlooks is the fact that medical expenses have gone up considerably since that time. A new situation has arisen with regard to medical expenses. Although it may have been a novelty to introduce this kind of tax relief in 1942 or 1943, we feel that it is a necessity today.
The parliamentary assistant makes a great deal out of the use of the word "normal" and 67509-44
Income Tax Act
contends that there are certain medical expenses that should be regarded as normal, even as food and clothing, and therefore should not be given special consideration in the matter of income tax deductibility. Mr. Speaker, it is precisely because not one of us would contend that every last article that some people might regard as medical expense-every last aspirin tablet, if you like -should be included; it is precisely for that reason that we feel that those medical expenses which the department does allow should be accorded deductibility right from the very first dollar. That is one way of dealing with the problem. If you cannot cover every last kind of expense, surely the kinds that are allowable should be allowed right from the first dollar.
I am interested in the extent to which the parliamentary assistant has raised the figure of what this proposal would cost. For the last year or two it has been said it would cost $35 million to $40 million to remove this floor. Today he said it would cost $50 million or $60 million. Of course prices are going up and medical costs are going up, and it may be that it would cost a bit more.

speechtext:
But the parliamentary assistant also, having given those figures, goes on to say that if that much money is to be given to the Canadian people by way of tax relief, the government is obliged to consider what is the best way in which to give that relief.
Well, the fact of the matter is that $30 million or $40 million or $50 million given as general tax relief spread over the whole population is such a small amount per week to the average taxpayer, such a few cents, it is not worth nearly as much as it would be to have the knowledge that in the case of medical expenses there would be more substantial relief. I submit that those who would not get 3 or 4 cents a week off their general tax because the money was not used for a general reduction would feel it was worth more to have the knowledge that in the event of high medical expenses the full amount of those expenses could be deducted for income tax purposes.
The parliamentary assistant to the minister gave the example of an income taxpayer at the $3,000 level for whom taxes had been reduced, if I took down his figures correctly, by $45 from 1952 to 1956. The parliamentary assistant gave $175 as the income tax in 1952 and $130 as the income tax in 1956, or a reduction of $45. This only underlines my point. At the $3,000 level that is a total tax reduction in four years of only 86 cents per

Income Tax Act
week, or a little over 20 cents per week per year. At the lower levels the reduction is even less than that.
The parliamentary assistant makes a great deal out of the fact that there are two million people in the working force who do not pay income taxes and therefore would not get any relief from the proposal I make. I do not know why he brings up the fact that in this country, which the Liberals boast is rolling in high gear, there are two million people in the working force whose incomes are so low they do not pay income taxes. This means that if they are single they are earning less than $1,000; if they are married without children they are earning less than $2,000; if they are married and have two children, they are earning less than $2,300 a year. I suggest it is a blot on the government of the day that it should allow, in this so-called fast rolling economy, so many people to be living on incomes as low as that.
The parliamentary assistant raised again the question of the way in which the resolution is worded, and the way in which a resolution such as this has to be treated by the government. He knows as well as anyone that a private member cannot word a resolution in such a way as to require the expenditure of money. All a private member can do is present a resolution that states the advisability of considering such a proposal. Most of us still feel that if the house as a whole approves of a resolution in those terms there is at least a moral obligation on the government to consider the matter, and to consider what very clearly must have been the views of the members when they passed such a resolution. I think it is well that once again we have an opportunity for the government to ascertain how members generally feel on this question.
The parliamentary assistant said there was one new item in the picture this year. I have already referred to it. It is the proposal made last week by the federal government at the conference with the provinces on the question of health insurance. As I have already indicated, I welcome the steps that have been taken. Naturally I do not believe the government's proposal goes far enough in this important field, but it goes a little farther than I thought this slow government might move by 1956.
The fact of the matter is that if the federal government's proposals come into effect in full there is still left for the individual Canadian the whole range of his doctor's and dentist's bills, a whole gamut of medical expenses that he will still have to pay on

an individual basis. Helpful though this proposed and welcome hospitalization scheme will be, there is still a wide range of medical expenses that will fall upon the individual, which still makes necessary the kind of consideration in respect of income tax that this resolution calls upon the government to give.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I urge the house to support this resolution asking for the removal of the 3 per cent floor with regard to the deductibility of medical expenses for income tax purposes.

Accident Prevention
I think this resolution is long overdue. When one looks at what has been happening to the children of Canada in the last few years -even the last few weeks-one will say it is high time that publicity be given to the need for the protection of our children.
We now have weeks for different things. We have a week for wild life, and in passing I should like to pay my tribute to men like Jack Miner who did so much to protect wild life in Canada, which work is being carried on by his family at the present time. But wild life, important as it is, fades into insignificance when compared with the lives of the boys and girls. Their lives are deathless and eternal.
I know we have many great things in Canada of which we are very proud. We have the greatest wheat growing fields in the world. We have the greatest wheat handling elevators in the world. We have the longest railroad in the world. We have the greatest fresh water lake in the world. We have the greatest mines in the world. But these fade into insignificance when compared with the lives of our boys and girls.
I have a chart here from which I obtained some vital statistics. It has a good deal to say about the death of children of various ages. For the whole of Canada in 1954 there were 124,520 deaths. Accident Prevention

There are many different causes of accidents. One is drowning. There are not many members in this house who do not know of a danger spot for little boys and girls. I can remember that one of the first things I had to do in Fort William was help Dr. Cook to give respiration to a little fellow who was drowned in the Neeking river. At the rear of the houses on the river there was nothing but a few willows to protect the boys and girls from drowning. On another occasion I saw a man sitting on the bank of Mosquito creek as I was coming in from the country on a Sunday afternoon. I asked, "What is the matter with you?" He said, "My boy went in swimming there," and you could not see a ripple of water. There was nobody to protect him or take him out. We got him out some time after.
Another cause of a good many accidents is cars and trucks. A little fellow will run out where you do not expect him to run. Sometimes accidents are caused by boys hitch-hiking on the rear of a car, or in the wintertime sliding behind the car. Many accidents occur when children are crossing the street. I can remember, not a great while ago, when a four-year old boy in Fort William ran out in front of a street car at a corner and lost his life.
Another outstanding cause of death of children is negligence and ill treatment by parents. When a father or mother indulges in drinking you might say they are not responsible, but they are responsible when the children suffer. Sometimes they leave them in an automobile while they go to a picture show or to a beer parlour. I must express my appreciation to the police of Fort William, because whenever they find a car with little children locked inside they take care of that car. Another thing children should be advised to do, especially little girls, is to be very careful in speaking to strange men. The tragic result of this has been seen in the past few days.
Another cause of accidents is fire. Sometimes this is the result of using matches; sometimes there are other causes. It is very difficult to save little children when a house is on fire. Another cause of accidents is the use of bicycles. When you are driving a car it is difficult to avoid a boy who swings out on a bicycle. Sometimes he will have another boy or perhaps two boys on the handlebar.
It is very difficult to protect the lives of those children. We know something of the importance of advertising. If the proper authorities in Canada would advertise a week for the protection of little folks it would go a long way to help. Fort William showed its
Accident Prevention
appreciation of the importance of advertising. Our chief of police and city council kept advertising the prevention of accidental death in Fort William for 629 days; now it has started again, and we hope the period will be longer this time.
A week for the protection of little folks should be advertised through our teachers, through our school boards, through our city councils, through our police forces, through our service clubs, through our churches and by means of women's auxiliaries.
I know the government showed its interest in the protection of little folks when it passed the Family Allowances Act. That is one of the greatest things that has ever been done to help the children of Canada. Some people think the allowances should be increased. I believe the minister would like to increase it, too, if he could get the means to do so. Another thing that is going to very much help the health and protection of little children is a new plan for health insurance. This health insurance will be of more benefit to children under 14 years of age than it will be to those over 14 years of age, because the death rate is so much higher.
Children's patrols and police patrols are doing good work in helping to protect the children at crossings. I noticed in the press today that the birth rate in Canada reached a new high in 1955; 442,000 in 1955 as compared with 435,000 in 1954.
I am not going to labour this very much longer, but I will say this. We can protect the lives of our boys and girls. We can protect their health, but we have to do something else. It is not sufficient to teach them how to earn a living; we must teach them how to live and how to honour their fathers and mothers, how to respect their Queen and country and to worship their God and serve Him daily. We must instil these ideas into their hearts and minds.
I place this resolution before you, Mr. Speaker, and I hope the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) will ensure that we have in Canada a week devoted to the protection of our little folks, because nothing in this country in the way of wealth or potential compares with our little boys and girls. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

The rights provided in section 148 shall be enjoyed without distinction of race, sex, religion or language and the right to vote in any election of members of parliament of Canada or the legislative assembly of any province shall not be denied or abridged on account of race, religion, language or sex.
150.	The rights conferred by sections 148 and 149 nereof of this act shall not be deemed to abridge any existing right of any person.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that section 150 is placed in the resolution so that beyond peradventure it would not be considered that the sections that precede it in any way limit the rights that have been established by law, by custom or by precedent to the citizens of Canada generally over the years.
Throughout the long history of the fight for human rights and freedom we have found from time to time the necessity of putting into writing the rights or the privileges that had been obtained or attained in former years by means of precedent. If we look through the pages of our Canadian history, as well as the history of the country from which we derive so many of our freedoms, Britain, I think we shall find that this is so. Often certain rights were established by custom; then later on it was thought wise by the people of the country and by the representatives whom they elected to their representative institutions, whether they were the parliaments of medieval times, the parliaments which followed the overthrow of the Stuart kings at the end of the 17th century, or more recently, to confer certain rights of representation and of voting upon various groups of people in our own
Human Rights
country and in the country from which we derive so much of our inspiration and so many of our institutions.
I might remark to the house that from time to time in this country over the years the right to vote has been limited by the action of legislatures because of race or religion. I only refer to measures that have been adopted by this parliament since I have been a member of this house in order sometimes to restore rights that had been abrogated, or to ensure rights that had been taken away by other legislatures.
It was not so long ago that persons professing a religion which caused some of the wilder men and women in that religious group to do things which were not in conformity with the manner in which we expect our citizens to behave-I refer of course to the Doukhobors-found that the right to vote for members of the parliament of Canada was based upon an enactment of the legislature of British Columbia. Because the province of British Columbia denied that group of people that right, they were denied the right to vote for representation in this parliament. I know of cases where the people on one side of the family were of Doukhobor descent and those on the other side were descendants of United Empire Loyalists; yet they were all denied the right to vote because they were said to be, and legally were, the descendants of Doukhobors.
I think it is wrong that this kind of thing should be done in connection with persons professing a certain religion, even though some disobey the law, provided the majority are law-abiding as is the case with the group I have just mentioned. In my own province of Saskatchewan we have large populations in some areas of people of Doukhobor origin, Doukhobor religion and Doukhobor descent. I venture to say that there are no more law-abiding citizens, there are no citizens who are becoming better integrated into our society in Saskatchewan than some of the descendants of those Doukhobor settlers who came to this country just before the dawn of the present century.
Consequently when any group of people are denied the right to exercise what we regard as the fundamental and basic rights of citizens, not only their rights but the rights of all citizens are to some degree endangered, because we never know when the denial of those rights may be extended to other groups within the community. Only a few days ago I was reading in the new issue of what is perhaps now the national magazine, Maclean's magazine, an editorial dealing with another religious group in one of our provinces which may be denied the right to hold

Human Rights
property as we understand that right. The editorial remarked that recently a group of municipal representatives in the province of Manitoba had approached the Manitoba government with the request that legislation be enacted similar to that which had been enacted in the province of Alberta several years ago to prevent people who professed a strange religion, who were considered to be a strange people, the Hutterites, from extending their holdings of land and establishing colonies I think within 40 miles of any existing colony.
The writer of that editorial pointed out very properly that if that kind of request were granted by the government of Manitoba -I say at once that the writer of the editorial was of the opinion that it would not be granted by the present government of Manitoba-it would constitute an infringement of a right which is implicit when we as a national parliament invite people to come to this country. When we allow people to come to Canada under our immigration regulations, if they are law-abiding people we should permit them the same basic rights as* the rest of us possess. No one will deny that the people to whom I have just referred are law-abiding.
In moving a resolution of this description. I have these recent matters and examples in mind. Then, too, I have noticed legislation recently introduced in one of the provinces in connection with the newsprint industry that might-I do not say it will-be used to limit the freedom of the press, that might be used indeed to stop the publication of a newspaper or a magazine which the authorities in that province did not like, which was violently opposed to the provincial regime. I say at once that I do not know that the legislation would be used for that purpose, but the obvious inference on reading the legislation is that it might be so used.
Then some years ago we had legislation, which was denied by the courts and the federal government, for the limitation of the freedom of the press in the province of Alberta; I refer to the provincial act of 1937.
Consequently it seems to me that we should have such rights of citizenship clearly set forth in our constitution. This resolution if accepted would write into our constitution some of these basic rights which are not written in at the present time. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) may say that the preamble of the British North America Act provides these rights, or perhaps by inference, custom or precedent there is an enjoyment of them; but I think I have already indicated several examples which would show that

these rights which are surely national in scope are not always respected by provinces and legislatures.
I am happy, of course, that from time to time our courts do interpret the constitution in such a manner as to safeguard some of our basic rights. The recent judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada in connection with the violation of a home by the police in a neighbouring province is a case in point. In that instance the final legal authority in this country, the Supreme Court of Canada, ruled that provincial police had acted in violation of the constitutional rights of a man who was holding a religious service in his home. They ruled also that in confiscating the literature and the Bible and deporting the man across the boundary they were infringing one of the basic rights of Canadian citizenship. So I say that from time to time our courts protect us by the interpretation of the law and the constitution.
Then, of course, there is undoubtedly discrimination as between individuals, sometimes on account of racial origin. It is very deplorable that in this province of Ontario, while the provincial legislature did pass an act making it an offence to discriminate against an individual because of his colour, that law has still been defied in one or two of the smaller places in Ontario and once or twice, indeed, I believe even in the city of Toronto. Racial discrimination does occur from time to time.
The Minister of Justice may say again, like the Minister of National Health and Welfare in another connection, that this might be considered as under provincial jurisdiction. Indeed, of course, some colour is given to that argument by the fact that several provinces have on the statute books legislation forbidding such discrimination. But it seems to me that we should have that protection as an inalienable right of our Canadian citizenship as such; not a right because we are residents of the province of Ontario, through a provincial act; or of the province of Saskatchewan, because of a provincial act; or of any other province because of a provincial act. We should have it as a constitutional right written into the constitution within a bill of rights.
That, as I have said, is one of the purposes of this resolution. Sometimes I have felt that even under our federal authority our immigration department has from time to time discriminated against persons who have come here, sometimes indeed ostensibly to do one thing when they may wish, having been here for some time, to remain to do another. I have felt that simply because they were of a different race or a different colour, they

have been deported. Of course I may be wrong in my judgment; I may be erring in that opinion; none the less that is my opinion, and I think it has been shared by a good many people who have looked into some of these cases in our country.
When we look around the world we see how from time to time in various other countries the rights of individuals have been abrogated or limited by the rise to power of persons who have no sympathy with human rights and fundamental freedoms. I know it will be said-perhaps the Minister of Justice will say it when he takes part in this discussion-that if you look across the sea, to the United Kingdom for example, you will find that the rights enjoyed by the people there are not embedded in a bill of rights, that they stem from a number of acts and a number of precedents.
Some of the precedents have been created by the courts. I have in mind at the moment the right to liberty of the individual, which was not originally set forth in any law but was expressed by Lord Mansfield. When it was brought to his attention that a negro-I have forgotten his name, but I think he was called James Somersett-was in slavery in England and was to be taken away again into slavery by his owner, the judge said something to this effect, "The air of this country is free, and he who breathes the air of this country must enjoy freedom." He ordered that slave to be set free. There was no bill of rights in the sense that I am discussing a bill of rights. There was no act of the British parliament which ensured to that individual the right to life and liberty, but he had that right by the judgment of a court. Subsequently the freedom of slaves was decreed by parliament.
It may be said, of course, that in the great country to the south they have written into their constitution a bill of rights; but you have only to look at what has happened there, particularly in the southern states recently, to realize it has not meant all that the persons who wrote that bill of rights intended it to mean when they wrote it into the constitution. However, I do not think that alters by one jot or tittle the fact that the writing into our constitution of a bill of rights of the description I have had the honour to place before the house tonight would imbed in our constitution, in the minds of our people, those basic rights of citizenship that are set forth, and give protection.
From time to time, of course, within recent years we have had the denial of the very first freedom I mention here; freedom of speech and expression. Under all sorts of
Human Rights
local enactments, sometimes municipal laws, persons who wished, shall we say, to conduct a religious service in the street were stopped from doing so; not only ordered to move on, but sometimes even arrested for causing obstruction.
Freedom of speech is a very precious thing which we enjoy under the constitution, and it should be specifically written in. Some of us have had the pleasure of strolling on an evening up to Hyde park corner and hearing the freedom of speech there under the protection of the law, in the person of a policeman. I remember when I was there in 1944 and the buzz bombs were coming over London, three Canadian friends and I walked one evening up to Hyde park corner, and we heard an agitator denouncing the war, denouncing the prime minister and the various political parties supporting the war, and calling the young men and women standing around fools for believing that the war was being fought for human freedom and human rights. Yet the policeman saw to it that the speaker was not interfered with.
That seemed to me, at least, to be going a very long way in freedom. None the less, because that freedom exists I believe that the rights of individuals in the United Kingdom and the institutions of that country are probably safer from violent overthrow than the institutions of almost any country in the world-not that I think that our own institutions are now in any danger in that respect. Freedom of speech and of expression are among the basic rights of the individual as is, of course, freedom of religion. Canadians belonging to one religious denomination regard people who attend religious services of other denominations not only with equanimity but with esteem and understanding, and that is a precious quality in the society in which we live.
I have already mentioned freedom of the press and of means of communication. I should also mention, of course, that right that has been secured after many years of struggle, the right to organize, the right to associate, and the right to express oneself with one's fellows through an organization and in association with people of like mind.
I have outlined other liberties in this resolution including freedom from cruel or unusual punishment. I do not think punishment of this kind is inflicted by any of the courts in this country. I do not know of a case in recent times which has brought a sentence of cruel or unusual punishment. I have sometimes thought, however, that the sentences meted out might have been more severe than was perhaps warranted by the crime; but even those punishments could not be characterized as cruel or unusual.

Within our own lifetime we have had instances of arbitrary arrest and detention, and within my experience in this house there have been instances of the denial of the right of the individual after arrest to be informed promptly of the charges against him and to be given a trial or released within a reasonable time. I am not going to go back and discuss in any detail the arrests that followed the Gouzenko episode, but I have always regarded what happened then as something of a blot on our Canadian jurisprudence, because some of the people who were picked up for questioning were held incommunicado, were not given access to legal counsel and were not charged with any crime. Although some of them were subsequently brought before the courts, found guilty and sentenced, others who had been treated in the same manner were found innocent. In that case, at least, there was a denial of justice of which most of us feel ashamed when we look back upon it.
Another right is that of habeas corpus. How often we have heard habeas corpus mentioned; yet I suppose there is no right we enjoy to which we are not heirs because of the descent of our constitution from that of Britain. The right of habeas corpus is the right of an individual to demand the production of someone who is under arrest, so that he may be brought before a proper court and given an opportunity to plead.
These are some of the rights I should like to see written into our constitution. It may be said, of course, that those rights are not in danger. However, tonight I have mentioned some of our rights which have been in danger or have actually been denied from time to time. It might be argued that the inclusion of these rights in the constitution of our country is wholly unnecessary, but I do not think so. Who knows what conditions may exist in this country at a future date? We have seen strange movements arise in some of the most progressive countries of the world. I know that 20 years ago I would not have thought it likely-indeed, I was going to put it more strongly and say I would not have thought it possible-that that democratic country in central Europe which was established after the first great war under President Masaryk would fall under dictatorship and become a totalitarian country. I would neither have thought that likely nor, as I said, possible; but that has happened. We do not know but that a group of individuals who would abrogate some of our basic freedoms-freedom of speech, of association, of the press, of religion and the freedom to vote
fMr. Coldwell.]
without regard to race, creed or colour

might obtain a sufficiently large following in the country to deny us the rights that go with Canadian citizenship.
It may be said, of course, that even if we write these freedoms into our constitution, such a group would set it aside. That may be true; none the less the very fact that these rights were written into our constitution and were regarded as basic rights would make it more difficult for them to dispense with those rights. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am again moving this resolution, not because I expect the Minister of Justice to accept it tonight in view of what he said last year, and not because I expect the house to adopt it if the minister opposes it tonight, but because I hope it will continue to be moved either by myself or by someone who may come after me until such time as a section somewhat like this is written into our constitution and becomes part of the permanent written constitution of this land.
I have sometimes been twitted because of the fact that I have given lectures in the past in which I said that I preferred an unwritten constitution to a written constitution. However, this is a country consisting of provinces, and it has a national, federal parliament. Consequently we had to have a written constitution. I would have been very happy indeed if the fathers of confederation had followed the inclination, shall I put it that way, of Sir John A. Macdonald and been able to establish a unitary form of government in this country. That was impossible, of course, because we had provinces that differed in their civil law, their conception of property rights and their desire to control- and quite properly-their educational facilities. Hence we could not have that. But I am quite sure that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the members of the government would have found the country much more easily governed had this been a unitary state instead of a federal state.
Because we are a federal state, I think it is more important that we should have written into our constitution a bill of rights of this description, so that we might not only limit our own power to abrogate the rights of citizenship within the provinces, but so the provinces should not have the right to abrogate the basic rights of national Canadian citizenship within their jurisdictions. So this resolution, if it became a bill which was introduced and passed, would limit the power of this parliament to deny any citizen any basic right, and by the same token it would also deny to legislative assemblies the right to abrogate any such right.

Incidentally, may I say this. I note that some legislative assemblies are now calling themselves provincial parliaments, and that certain premiers of provinces are now calling themselves prime ministers. According to my reading of the British North America Act, I thought there was to be one parliament of Canada; and by the same token I should think there would be but one Prime Minister of Canada. I make that comment incidentally, because this innovation has struck me as another one of those attempts to lower the prestige of the Prime Minister and of the parliament of Canada by placing the legislative assemblies and their premiers on the same level as that of the parliament of Canada and the office of the first or principal adviser of Her Majesty the Queen within Canada.
I want to conclude, Mr. Speaker, by thanking the house for giving me its attention again. I may say that I did not come down here tonight expecting to move this resolution. However, I discovered that there were some who expected me to move it. Their resolutions coming next, I found that I would have gravely embarrassed them if I had failed to move this resolution. I am therefore commending it to the Minister of Justice and the house. If not tonight or if not at this session, I hope that on some future occasion, even in some future session, such a bill of rights will be adopted and become part of the accepted constitution of this great, free land which we want to maintain in freedom and in peace.

It is because of the fact that I endorse his sentiments that I deprecate that he of all people in this house should seek to change an essential characteristic of the Canadian constitution which we have inherited from Great Britain, namely the principle of the sovereignty of parliament, and in its stead to adopt the type of bill of rights which they have in the United States constitution and which, if I understood him correctly this evening, he himself does not admire in all its parts.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENSURE FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will permit me to say so, I think he misses the real point entirely. It is not a question of whether the United States constitution is a written one and the British largely unwritten so much as it is a question of whether, in a British democracy, we the people have sufficient confidence in our own judgment as democrats and sufficient confidence in our own legislative assemblies that we are not afraid to trust ourselves and our children, and our representatives in parliament to reach wise decisions. If we do not trust them, and if we do not trust the processes of democracy in our country, then we shall seek to restrict and hedge in the powers of the elected representatives of the people, as is done in the United States constitution.
On the occasion on which this matter has been discussed previously I attempted to make the point that if we could look around us in the world and see any written constitution such as that which as my hon. friend advocates restricts the powers of its legislative assembly, and if we could see that in practice it really protected the liberties of the subject, then I would say by all means adopt it. But I suggest to my hon. friend that he will look around the world in vain for any country whose constitution is restricted by a bill of rights which provides even a fraction of the protection of human rights and liberties that we are very proud to possess in the British countries, and specifically in Canada.
Now, my hon. friend from Rosetown-Biggar has referred to the British North America Act, and correctly, because that written statute is the main part of our Canadian constitution. He will see that in the very first paragraph of the preamble to that statute it says:
Whereas the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick have expressed their desire to be federally united into one dominion under the crown of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, with a constitution similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom:
I say, Mr. Speaker, that following the passage of that imperial act it is a matter of history that in this country we have enjoyed all the traditional freedoms of British people. We have enjoyed them, if the comparison is not an invidious one-and certainly my hon. friend will not say it is invidious-to a far greater extent than those same freedoms have been enjoyed by any country anywhere in the world under the type of written constitution with a bill of rights which he would like to foist upon us.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar says that the difference between our country and Great Britain in this respect is that Great
[Mr. Coldwell.l
Britain-he is quite right in this-has a unitary government, while in this country we have a federal system in which the total powers of government are divided between those which have to do with the national or federal government at Ottawa, and which are under the authority of this parliament, and those which have to do with the provinces, and which are properly under the control of the various provincial legislatures.
He said it is because of this division of authority that we should have in our constitution the same principles which they have in the United States constitution, whereby the successfully rebelling citizens of the United States colonies withheld from their national congress and state legislatures certain rights which they, the people, hold unto themselves and have not seen fit to bestow upon the national congress and government or the state legislatures and governments. If we are going to follow my hon. friend's advice in this matter, our problem is that of transforming the British principle of the sovereignty of parliament and provincial legislatures in the federal state of Canada in the form in which it was created by grafting upon our Canadian constitution, with its divided authority between Canada and the provinces, a bill of rights characteristic of the United States system. I say to my hon. friend with great respect that far from the fact that our constitution is a federal constitution being a good reason why we should adopt this suggestion of his, the very opposite is the case.
He says in his resolution:
That, in the opinion of this house, consideration should be given to the taking of whatever steps are necessary to amend the British North America Act so as to include therein the following heading and sections:
Let me point out to my hon. friend what we should have to do in order to take the necessary steps referred to in the language I have just quoted. As we all know, under the British North America Act the entire powers of government in Canada have been divided up between those matters which are specifically assigned to the provinces as being of more provincial and local character, and those specific powers which are assigned to the dominion parliament. In addition, there is a general power assigned to this parliament to make laws relating to all those matters which are not specifically assigned to the provinces.
The very first power which was assigned to the provinces when the British North America Act was passed was:
1. The amendment from time to time, notwithstanding anything in this act, of the constitution of the province, except as regards the office of lieutenant governor.

My hon. friend, who is anxious to see that there should be included in the British North America Act some restraint upon the scope of the powers of the provinces in order to make it impossible for the provincial legislatures and governments to do some of the things which have been done and which he deprecates, might be well advised to address his arguments to the provincial legislatures in question themselves. They have the power to change their constitutions as long as they confine it to matters which are of purely provincial concern, and do not attempt to deal with the office of lieutenant governor.
The hon. member will recall that back in 1949 this parliament took the power, which we had not previously had, to pass laws dealing with all those matters which were of purely federal concern. But after we had done so, the British North America Act still dealt with a third class of matters, namely matters of joint concern to the federal parliament and the provincial legislature. In respect of that third group I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that while it is true the parliament at Westminster throughout the years has seen fit to pass amendments to the British North America Act upon the receipt of a joint address of the Senate and the House of Commons, it would be politically difficult, if not unthinkable, that a responsible federal government should introduce such a joint address into the Senate and the House of Commons as would abrogate in any way the powers of the provincial governments over matters of joint concern unless the provinces concurred in that action.
I should think that, having regard to the fact that over the years the courts have unanimously held that the provinces acting within the sphere of their authority are just as sovereign as this parliament, it would not contribute very greatly to the political or constitutional harmony of this country if we in this parliament were to take it upon ourselves to follow the advice which I am sure my hon. friend either urges or implies by his resolution and by the speech with which he has supported it.

Human Rights

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE TO ENSURE FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. With great deference to my hon. friend, if he will forgive me for saying so, I say it is a misunderstanding of some of these points, such as the one he just made, that causes him to have the desire to move the resolution he has moved tonight.
If I understand his question correctly, I should say this. The principle of the sovereignty of parliament, which is one of the cardinal principles of the British constitution, became the right and privilege of this house in respect of matters under its jurisdiction, and of the provincial legislatures in matters under their jurisdiction. Hence, much as we may regret it when cases arise such as my hon. friend mentioned, they fall within the principle of sovereignty of parliament of the British constitution and of our own constitution. It is within these principles that these acts that my hon. friend mentioned are passed. The only way in which this can be prevented-and he is perfectly right on this point-is by attaching to our constitution, both for the provinces and for this parliament, the same type of restrictions that he himself says are unsatisfactory in their operation as part of the bill of rights of the United States constitution.
My contention is, as it has been on previous occasions, that with all our Canadian constitution's faults, and they are not many; with every fault that my hon. friend can name, the provisions we have in the British North America Act are so superior to any of the types of bills of rights that my hon. friend can bring forward that I do not think we should compare them as being in the same class.
I grant you that on paper it sounds very impressive to say that no man shall be deprived of his property without due process of law; but I am sure my hon. friend's idealism would get a great shock if he were to look at the law reports and find in them many public utility cases in which the citizens invoking this provision of the bill of rights were large power corporations which said that they could not be brought under the type of act that my hon. friend himself might think was a very good act to pass, upon the argument that it was not within the power of that legislature to pass a law that took away from that power corporation the least part of its property or rights unless the matter were put before some court, and there disposed of by what they argued was due process of law.
My hon. friend has made reference to certain cases that he thinks are regrettable. I am now expressing solely my own views. Perhaps it is desirable, if we are engaged

Human Rights
in a life and death struggle with people who are bitterly opposed in every respect to every political concept that we hold dear, we should not shackle our own legislative powers to deal with any emergency that might arise in such time of war. For all of the abuses that may have arisen in that respect in countries like Great Britain, Australia and Canada, that have this principle of sovereignty of parliament, I am sure there are dozens of abuses that could be cited in other countries with bills of rights; where for example the right to vote is guaranteed to millions of citizens who have never received it. It is for that reason, Mr. Speaker, I find it rather hard to understand why my hon. friend from Rosetown-Biggar should be urging what, in my view, is so foreign to those views which I have always 'understood him to possess.
I am sure he and I share together a very deep-seated admiration and respect for all the political institutions of the United Kingdom which we have inherited in the British North America Act, and which today are one of our greatest treasures. It would be a matter of the very greatest regret to introduce anything into our constitution which would make it less like that of the great country from which we inherited it, and more like those with constitutions containing bills of rights with whose operation in real life we are all so familiar.
On the last occasion on which this was discussed the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar will recall that I read into the record what I think without question, as those constitutions go, was perhaps on paper the most admirable extant. It is one of the most recent. The scholars who drew it up could examine those that existed before and bring down a really perfect protection for the liberties of the citizens.
As he will recall, on that occasion it sounded so good that one hon. member thought it was something prepared under the auspices of the United Nations. Actually it was the constitution of the Byelorussian republic. The hon. gentleman can see from this that it is all very well to draw up those constitutions on paper, but so far as the actual protection they give to citizen John Doe when his liberties are invaded, if we reflect for one moment we shall realize at once that that protection has to come from the invocation of the law by the law enforcement authorities that may result in an action before perhaps not a high court judge but merely a police magistrate. And so far as John Doe is concerned at that particular juncture, the protection of his liberty will not be one bit better than the interpretation by that magistrate of the law
tMr. Garson.l
that is applicable to his case. If the law enforcement authorities are strongly opposed to the law that they are being asked to invoke, they will invoke it with something less than enthusiasm. The results for John Doe may be as if that law had never existed. If my hon. friend from Rosetown-Biggar thinks this is an exercise of my imagination I say, look at thousands of cases that have arisen under these bills of rights such as he advocates, and see if that is not the case in actual fact.
Where are the franchises which millions of citizens should have had and which for decades they have not enjoyed? Why is that, if it is not because there is no machinery or no organization to which they can go to have their rights under these bills of rights enforced? Therefore when my hon. friend brings along his motion and says we need this bill of rights because we are a federal state, that we should embark upon an application to the imperial parliament at Westminster to amend the British North America Act, in order to take away or abridge those powers of the provinces that I have mentioned here of amending their own constitutions, and to take away or abridge or limit in many ways their present powers over the administration of justice and the enforcement of the law, to interfere with their jurisdiction over property and civil rights, are we to be so naive that we should think that after we have done that, we can go back to those same provincial governments and legislatures which cherish their powers and jurisdiction just as much as we do ours in this parliament; these powers over which we shall have run roughshod and we can then go back to them and ask if they will enforce those new laws that we have passed?
Therefore when my hon. friend says that because we have a federal state, that is the reason we should seek this change, I say to him that if we have any practical political sense whatever we will know that where there is this division of authority between Canada and the provinces it is of supreme importance that any change we make in our constitution will carry the judgment not only of this parliament and this government but of all the provincial authorities who have to enforce any changes that we may seek or get.
As regards the ideals that my hon. friend has set up, we are not in disagreement. I do not think a safety razor blade could be put between his views and mine as to the importance of the civil liberties of the individual. I think the difference between us is that I personally do not think there is any use trying to bring about a new heaven on earth unless

we pay some attention to the methods by which we are going to do that. All I have ever attempted to reply to a proposal such as that of my hon. friend in this same sort of context in which we are debating tonight, is this. You wish these principles protected. They are protected now by the British method. But you say we should protect them by the United States method. Let us then look at what we have to do in order to import this United States method into our Canadian constitution.
When we come to that point it has seemed to me-I have stated this on previous occasions-that it would be an act of very great unwisdom indeed if we should attempt in this parliament or under any federal auspices to take away any of the rights of the provinces, even if we thought they should be taken away.
For I put this to my hon. friend. Once you have this division of authority between the central government and the provincial governments in a free federal state-this does not apply to the U.S.S.R.; it applies to" Australia, where they have these problems to just as great or a greater degree than we have them here-if we are going to seek for any practical solution to this matter of a bill of rights, the only way in which we can find it is if we seek it in co-operation with the provincial authorities. For as long as they retain under our constitution, which my hon. friend admires so much, the exclusive authority over the administration of justice and the enforcement of the law, we are going to be dependent upon their actions for the effectiveness of any changes in the law we make by securing a bill of rights.

It is not extraneous at all. If I have a few minutes to finish my remarks, I would refer again to what I have said on previous occasions. While these are variations on the theme-I try to keep my theme exactly the same-the theme is that there is no
Human Rights
objection at all to examining my hon. friend's suggestions in this country, but the only effective way in which they can be examined is by the federal authorities in concern with all the provincial authorities examining them. No other way is effective. That is what I ventured to suggest on previous occasions and that is what I suggest on the present occasion.
I admit that the point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is well taken, but in order to fill in this gap in the resolution, and perhaps in my own remarks, I say that we must act together if we are going to accomplish any proper or satisfactory results.

subtopic: MEASURE TO ENSURE FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS

speechtext: Would the minister permit a question? Has the government given consideration to the resumption of the federal-provincial conference on constitutional questions?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE TO ENSURE FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has not given consideration to a resumption of the federal-provincial conference on constitutional amendments. That had to do entirely with the method or means by which we might bring into existence in Canada, without resorting to the imperial parliament at Westminster, the means of amending our Canadian constitution entirely in Canada in a way that was approved by the federal parliament and certain suggested alternative numbers of provinces.
Whether it might be difficult to arrive at a method of amending the constitution in Canada, it might still be possible to deal with the distinct problem or point which has been raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and reach agreement with the provincial authorities concerning the insertion of a bill of rights in our constitution. If the provinces approved this it could take the form of a request to the imperial parliament to pass an amendment to the British North America Act under our present method. It was in that sense that I was saying in reply to the interjection made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and to the mover of this resolution, that this is a matter that could be given consideration, but only satisfactorily by joint action of the federal and provincial authorities.
